summary: Light on Chappaquiddick's northeast point, first lit 1801; the wooden tower standing today dates from 1893 and was moved inland as the cliff eroded.

structures.note: Keeper's dwelling, two stories, erected for $12,000 (nomination); no longer standing per LighthouseFriends

access.note: Reached through the Cape Poge Wildlife Refuge (Trustees of Reservations). Pedestrians enter free; vehicles need an oversand permit. LighthouseFriends says the tower is open during guided tours; check before going.

facts.agency: U.S. Coast Guard (owner, per the Trustees' page and LighthouseFriends); The Trustees of Reservations (refuge and tours)

events.note: Keeper Matthew Mayhew activated the light in December 1801 (LighthouseFriends); the nomination dates the first tower to 1802
First tower, 35 ft, wooden, shingled, iron lantern (nomination; LighthouseFriends gives 1801)
Lamps and reflectors replaced by an array of oil lamps and reflectors supplied by Winslow Lewis
Light extinguished on orders in the War of 1812 and relit in early 1815 (LighthouseFriends)
Nomination: old tower lost with the eroding shoreline and a new one set back. LighthouseFriends: the 1801 tower was being moved a few yards back in 1838
New tower finished in July 1844, joined to the keeper's dwelling by a walkway (LighthouseFriends); Trustees also give 1844 as a rebuilding year
Two-story keeper's dwelling erected, $12,000 (nomination)
Fourth-order Fresnel lens replaced the lamps and reflectors; a new lantern room installed (LighthouseFriends; USLHS record gives 1857)
Light moved 40 feet to a new tower, 26 June 1893 (Light-House Board report for fiscal 1893); nomination says set back 35 ft in 1892; LighthouseFriends says a 35-foot wooden tower built 40 ft inland
Iron railing put in place on the deck around the lantern, and minor repairs
From fixed white to flashing white and red, because the beacon was confused with the Cross Rip Lightship's light (LighthouseFriends)
Boathouse rebuilt and enlarged; oil house built; quarters rearranged
Tower moved 50 feet (LighthouseFriends)
Keeper Thomas and assistant King towed a disabled motor boat with a man, a woman and a child to Edgartown, 12 July
Thomas and Smith helped float the sloop-yacht Ladrone of New York and the yacht Dolly of Boston, both aground near the station; Dolly commended for 22 July
Tower moved to its present location (nomination); LighthouseFriends gives a 95-foot move
Earthquake of 28 February 1925: the lighthouse swayed and the rotation of the light stopped for a time
Thomas assisted a disabled motor boat that drifted off course during the gale of 16 and 17 November
Automated when Joseph H. Dubois was keeper (USLHS record; LighthouseFriends)
Light made unattended in 1946; Henry S. Brown given as last keeper (LighthouseFriends; roster runs to 1946)
Tower moved 150 feet (LighthouseFriends)
Tower moved 500 feet inland by U.S. Army helicopter; the nomination had planned a 500-foot move in 1986 (LighthouseFriends; nomination)
Lantern room removed by helicopter 6 October 1997, restored in New Bedford, returned 16 December 1997 (LighthouseFriends)

Drifted off course in the gale of 16 and 17 November; assisted by keeper Henry L. Thomas

corrections.why: The tower standing today is the third on the site and dates from 1893. The 1801 date belongs to the first tower (LighthouseFriends dates the light to 1801; the nomination to 1802).
The USLHS record gives the tower as 35 feet (10.7 m); LighthouseFriends gives 35 feet.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record's 1801 build date is the first tower. The 1893 move (Light-House Board report, fiscal 1893) and the nomination's 1893 tower identify the standing tower.

notes_for_editor: Unresolved: (1) first tower, 1801 (LighthouseFriends, Mayhew lit it in Dec 1801; USLHS 1801) against 1802 (nomination); (2) land price $36 (LighthouseFriends) against $30 (nomination OCR, '?30.00', hard to read); (3) the optic change: nomination says reflectors replaced by revolving red and white prisms 1853-59; LighthouseFriends and USLHS say a fourth-order Fresnel in 1857; (4) move distance and date: Light-House Board says 40 feet on 26 June 1893, nomination says 1892 set back 35 feet, LighthouseFriends 40 feet inland; (5) 1898 flashing white and red change is LighthouseFriends only: the 1899 Light-House Board volume read here has no entry for Cape Poge characteristic; (6) automation 1943 (USLHS, LighthouseFriends) against keeper Henry S. Brown in the roster to 1946 and LighthouseFriends' 1946 unattended date; (7) relocation: nomination planned 1986; LighthouseFriends says 1987 by helicopter; (8) maintenance: Trustees' page says Coast Guard maintains the tower; LighthouseFriends says Trustees since 1994; (9) range: Trustees say nine miles, unit not given; record's 9.0 nm not used. OCR notes: the 1919 Bulletin PDF p. 31 OCR is badly broken, so the rescue detail is supported in the quote list by the 1918-1923 index (rescue 87) and the Bulletin text read locally; the 1915 Commissioner table names were matched by column position (fiscal 1915, saving of life). The Chronicling America searches for Cape Poge in Massachusetts papers, 1880-1930, found no lighthouse-keeper page. LSS 1880 recommended a station at Cape Poge; no source read here shows one being built, so the story does not say it was. Keeper Henry S. Brown's 1945 to 1946 span and the 1943 automation are both kept as the sources give them. Checked on page images in the fact-check (2026-10-22): the NRHP chronology page (PDF p. 11, form page 3) reads '$30.00' for the 1801 land, confirming the nomination's figure; the 1915 Commissioner table (scan p. 65, printed p. 60) reads the Barrus and Hopkins line and the two rescues in the 2nd-district rows as stated; the 1919 Bulletin PDF p. 31 (printed p. 87) reads 'On July 12 H. L. Thomas ... P. S. King ... man, woman, and child'; the FY1922 report (scan p. 752, printed p. 52) reads 'Ladrone, of New York' where the OCR reads 'Ixidrone'; the 1925 Bulletin PDF p. 15 (printed p. 73) reads the 28 February shock and 'about five minutes'. Printed page numbers for the 1893 and 1894 Light-House Board entries are not confirmed, so the story cites scan pages. LighthouseFriends says 'James' was promoted to head keeper in 1882 where the USLHS roster says Jethro Worth; the story follows the roster and does not repeat the LighthouseFriends name.
